Spring4Shell used SQL injection
explain: Denylists fail open when the platform changes underneath them. The module system created a new route to the class loader. Binding allowlists, as in the fixed code, do not have this problem.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Detecting server-side attacks and the defence map
question: A team can do only one thing this quarter. Which control reduces the impact of the widest range of server-side attacks, including ones not yet discovered?
options: Default-deny egress from application servers, with an allowlist and logging
A WAF rule for each new CVE
Renaming admin URLs
Disabling HTTP/2
explain: Egress control breaks SSRF to internal hosts, XXE and Log4Shell callbacks and many exfiltration paths, and its denials are evidence. WAF rules lag behind each new variant; renaming URLs is obscurity, not control.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Compressed FSMs: decoding several tokens in one step
question: Why does SGLang retokenize after a jump instead of appending the jumped string's own tokens?
options: Retokenizing is the only way to compute logits
The jumped string has no tokens until the detokenizer runs
Tokenizing the jumped piece alone can give splits the model rarely saw (summa plus ry), shifting its next-token distribution; retokenizing keeps the context close to normal
To make the KV cache smaller
explain: Models are trained on canonical BPE tokenizations. A non-canonical boundary changes the input the model conditions on. The paper and blog retokenize the text to keep it aligned, at a small cost.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Prefill-decode disaggregation and speculative decoding in SGLang
question: For which deployment is enabling EAGLE-3 in SGLang most likely to cut per-user latency?
options: A batch scoring job at very high concurrency that already saturates the GPU's compute
A service where every request has a different grammar and short outputs
A PD deployment whose bottleneck is the 25 Gb/s KV link
A coding assistant with few concurrent users producing long, fairly predictable completions
explain: Speculation spends spare compute in memory-bound decode steps. At low concurrency there is plenty, and predictable text keeps acceptance high. A compute-saturated batch job has no spare compute, short outputs give little to accelerate, and a slow KV link limits TTFT, which speculation does not touch.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
question: After contraction, an important motorway is closed and its weight becomes very large. What happens to a plain CH built for the old weights?
options: Queries remain correct, since shortcuts are recomputed during each query
Shortcuts that include the motorway now carry stale weights, so the contraction (at least the weights) must be redone
Only the node order must change; shortcut weights update themselves
Nothing changes, because CH queries ignore original arc weights
explain: Shortcut weights are sums of original arc weights fixed at preprocessing time. The survey notes CH can keep its node order and rerun contraction for a new metric, but some recomputation is unavoidable. Handling frequent weight changes cheaply is what customizable methods target (next lesson).

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The FFT: from N squared to N log N with butterflies
question: How many butterflies does a radix-2 FFT of N = 8 samples perform?
explain: There are log2 8 = 3 stages and each stage has N/2 = 4 butterflies, so 12 in total. 64 is the number of multiply-adds in the direct DFT (N squared), and 24 is N log2 N, which counts outputs over all stages (8 per stage), two per butterfly.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
question: Your Neon float sum with one accumulator runs exactly 4x faster than scalar, never more, even on data in L1. What is the most likely next step?
options: Use 4 to 8 independent accumulators and combine them at the end
Switch to 512-bit vectors
Align the array to 64 bytes
Add -O3
explain: Both the scalar and the 1-accumulator loops are bound by add latency: one add per chain per latency period. Independent accumulators overlap the chain; on the measured M5 Pro that took 4.5x to 15.5x.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
question: A loop over an array of 64-byte structs reads one float field per struct. AVX2 intrinsics give almost no speedup. What is the most effective first change?
options: Use AVX-512 instead
Store that field in its own contiguous array (struct-of-arrays) so one load brings 8 useful floats
Add more accumulators
Use target_clones
explain: With array-of-structs, each useful float sits 64 bytes from the next, so a vector needs a gather or 8 separate loads and wastes most of each cache line. A separate float array gives contiguous vector loads and 16 floats per cache line.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: How Linux stacks them, and how to choose
question: A game allocates thousands of temporary objects while building each frame, and none of them is needed after the frame is drawn. Which allocator fits best?
options: A buddy allocator, so the temporary objects can merge back into big blocks
A slab cache per object type, so each object can be freed individually
The general-purpose malloc, because the objects have different sizes
A per-frame bump arena that is reset after the frame is drawn
explain: All objects share one lifetime that ends at a known point, which is exactly the phase-oriented pattern bump allocation is built for: each allocation is a pointer add and freeing the whole frame is one reset.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Low-precision rollout: FP8 weights, FP8 KV cache and INT4
question: In a BF16-train, FP8-rollout run, a teammate says `--hf-checkpoint` only seeds SGLang at startup, so after the first sync it no longer matters what it points to. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing: weight sync always ships bf16 and SGLang quantizes on load
--hf-checkpoint is where Megatron loads its training weights from
SGLang reloads --hf-checkpoint from disk after every sync
The trainer reads quantization_config from that checkpoint's config.json and uses it to quantize the trained weights at every sync
explain: The weight updater is created with the quantization_config of --hf-checkpoint, and quantize_params applies it to every bucket. Megatron trains from --ref-load or --load, not from the HF checkpoint, and SGLang receives tensors rather than rereading the file (except in disk transport, which writes a new checkpoint).

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Launching and debugging a slime run
question: Generations look like garbage, and you suspect either the FP8 rollout checkpoint or the weight sync. Which first step isolates the inference side cheaply?
options: Run with `--debug-train-only`
Run with `--debug-rollout-only` on a few GPUs to see whether SGLang alone generates coherent text from the checkpoint
Increase `--global-batch-size`
Disable `--colocate`
explain: The debug guide suggests `--debug-rollout-only` with few GPUs to test the quantized checkpoint alone; if it is fine, look at the sync with `--check-weight-update-equal`.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Ethereum accounts, transactions and gas
question: What does an EOA's nonce protect against?
options: Someone rebroadcasting the same signed transaction to run it twice
Reentrancy into a contract
Running out of gas
Front-running in the mempool
explain: Each nonce can be used once per account, so a copy of an already-executed signed transaction is invalid. Contracts that accept signed messages need their own nonces for the same reason (lesson 12).

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Integer overflow, rounding and precision
question: In Solidity 0.8, `uint256 x = 3; x -= 5;` runs outside any unchecked block. What happens?
options: The transaction reverts with Panic 0x11
x becomes 2^256 - 2
x becomes 0
The compiler rejects the code
explain: Checked arithmetic is the default since 0.8.0. Wrapping (2^256 - 2) is what happens inside unchecked or before 0.8. The compiler cannot know runtime values, so it compiles.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Signatures on chain: replay, nonces and EIP-712 domains
question: Which EIP-712 domain field stops a signature for vault A from being accepted by vault B on the same chain?
options: chainId
version
verifyingContract
name
explain: verifyingContract binds the signature to one contract address. chainId separates chains; name and version separate apps and releases but two deployments of the same code share them.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Finding bugs early: review, static analysis, fuzzing, formal methods
question: The fuzzer reports '200 runs x 8 steps: invariant held' for a new contract. What can you conclude?
options: No sequence the fuzzer tried broke the invariant; untested sequences and properties remain open
The contract is proven safe
The contract needs no audit
The invariant must be wrong
explain: Fuzzing samples the input space. It raises confidence and finds bugs fast, but only formal verification against a correct specification covers all inputs, and neither checks properties nobody wrote.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The four triage questions, and the decision flow they make
question: An alert says "login from new country" for a user, but the raw event shows the country field is empty and the SIEM's geolocation lookup defaulted to the first entry in its table. Which question caught this, and what is the right action?
options: Question 1; tune the rule to ignore that user
Question 3; ask the user whether they travelled
Question 4; escalate because geolocation failures can hide attacks
Question 2, the data is wrong; fix the enrichment or parser and note that the rule fired on bad data
explain: The data is wrong, so the user's behaviour has not been shown to be unusual at all. Microsoft Sentinel even has a separate closing reason for this, false positive due to incorrect data. The fix belongs to the pipeline, and the note tells the engineers what broke.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Malware on an endpoint: reading a process tree
question: Your tree-building script links children to parents by ParentProcessId. Which bug will it produce?
options: None; PIDs are unique for the life of the machine
It will run too slowly
It will skip all processes started by SYSTEM
A child whose parent has exited can be attached to a later, unrelated process that reused the parent's PID, producing a false lineage
explain: Windows recycles PIDs, which is why Sysmon adds ProcessGuid. In the example, notepad.exe reused cmd.exe's PID 7312. Linking by PID can fabricate a malicious-looking tree, or hide a real one.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Pivoting, building a timeline, and mapping it to ATT&CK
question: You pivot from a malicious IP to proxy logs and find no other host contacted it in the last 7 days. What should the case note say?
options: Nothing, since the search found nothing
That the scope is bounded: the exact query, the time range and that no other host connected, so others can trust (or extend) the check
That the IP is safe
That the proxy logs must be broken
explain: Negative results are findings. Recording the exact query and range lets IR rely on it, or rerun it over a longer window. It says nothing about the IP being safe.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Metrics, burnout and the analyst's ethics
question: A manager asks you to pull a list of websites their employee visited last week "to check if they're working". There is no case number. What do you do?
options: Run the query; managers can see their team's data
Run it but only share the top ten sites
Ask the employee for permission first
Decline and point them to the formal process (HR and legal), because the SOC's access exists to detect malicious or abusive behaviour, not for performance monitoring outside a sanctioned process
explain: This is the NCSC's example almost word for word. Monitoring for performance is a separate, policy-governed matter; using SOC access for it outside that process breaches least access and purpose limits.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Password and MFA friction: rules that backfire and rules that work
question: A company's push-based MFA is being bombed with prompts. As an interim step before phishing-resistant MFA, which change does CISA recommend?
options: Lock the account after one denied prompt
Send prompts by SMS instead
Ask users to approve only during business hours
Enable number matching so approving requires typing the number shown on the real login screen
explain: Number matching ties approval to the login screen the real user is looking at, so blind or accidental approvals stop working. SMS is weaker, and time-of-day rules do not stop a determined attacker.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Designing help-desk verification that holds under pressure
question: Why does the policy require two independent proofs for privileged accounts even after a successful video check?
options: Video calls are slow
Privileged users are more often impostors
A single proof can be faked or stolen, and a privileged account can change the identity system itself
Managers always approve requests
explain: The impact of a wrong decision is highest for admins (Okta's cases), and synthetic video weakens video checks. Two proofs through different channels mean an attacker must defeat both.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Badges, readers and tailgating
question: An office uses cards that send a fixed number to every reader. Which upgrade addresses cloning directly?
options: Printing photos on the cards
Cards that sign a fresh random challenge with a private key that never leaves the chip
Longer card numbers
Moving readers to the inside of the doors
explain: A fixed number, however long, can be read once and replayed. A signature over a new challenge each time cannot be produced from recordings of earlier exchanges.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: A reporting culture, and what to do when someone is fooled
question: According to NCSC's Principle 2, why must people feel safe from negative repercussions?
options: So that the security team can skip investigations
Because otherwise they hide mistakes and stop reporting, removing the early warning
Because the law requires it
So that phishing tests can be harder
explain: NCSC says without psychological safety people fall into self-preserving behaviour such as covering up mistakes, which is the opposite of what detection needs.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
question: Your 4M-latent SAE has 40% dead latents. Which change directly gives those latents a training signal?
options: Increase lambda so the remaining latents are sparser
Decrease the batch size
Remove the decoder bias
Add an auxiliary loss that reconstructs the main SAE's residual error using only the dead latents' top activations
explain: A dead latent gets no gradient from the main loss because it never fires. AuxK forces the top k_aux dead latents to predict the residual error, giving them gradient toward directions the live latents miss. Increasing lambda would push even more latents off.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Where SAEs fall short: absorption, missing features and weak baselines
question: A 65k-latent SAE has a 'starts with E' latent that fires on almost every E-word except ' elephant', where an 'elephant' latent fires alone. What is the most likely explanation and fix?
options: The latent is dead on ' elephant'; add AuxK
Feature absorption: the elephant latent's decoder includes the 'starts with E' direction. Try a Matryoshka SAE, or check recall against a probe
Shrinkage from the L1 penalty; switch to TopK
The model does not know that elephant starts with E
explain: A hierarchy (elephant implies starts-with-E) lets sparsity merge the parent direction into the child latent, leaving a hole in the parent latent. Going wider or sparser tends to make it worse; nested Matryoshka losses penalise it. AuxK only helps latents that never fire.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights
question: The ordinary kriging system has an extra row of ones and an extra unknown $\mu$. What would go wrong if you dropped them and just solved $\Gamma \boldsymbol\lambda = \boldsymbol\gamma_0$?
options: The weights would no longer be forced to sum to 1, so the estimate would be biased whenever the unknown mean is not zero
Nothing; the row only speeds up the solve
The estimate would ignore the nearest sensor
The matrix would become 8 by 8
explain: The constraint row enforces $\sum_i \lambda_i = 1$, which makes the estimate unbiased for any constant mean. Without it the weights can sum to anything, and the estimate is pulled toward or away from zero.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Draft, verify, keep: the loop with greedy decoding
question: Why does the target pass produce gamma + 1 distributions rather than gamma?
options: Causal attention gives a next-token distribution after every input token, including after the last guess, which supplies a bonus token when all guesses pass
One extra position is needed to check the prefix
The draft also returns one distribution that is reused
It is an implementation detail that is never used
explain: The forward pass over prefix plus gamma guesses outputs a distribution after each of them. The last one, after guess gamma, is a free target prediction used only when all guesses are accepted, raising the maximum to gamma + 1 tokens per round.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
question: In multi-step speculative sampling, child 1 was rejected. A teammate tests child 2 with min(1, p(x)/q(x)) using the original p. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; every child is compared with the same target p
Child 2 should be compared with q only
After the rejection the output must follow the residual p1, so child 2 must be tested against p1; using p over-weights tokens the draft over-proposes
Child 2 should always be accepted after a rejection
explain: The rejection already spent the accepted mass min(p, q). What remains to be produced is the residual p1 = norm(max(0, p - q)). Testing against p would add min(p, q) a second time, the same double counting as resampling from p in lesson 3.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculation in a serving system: batch size, long context and tuning
question: A chat service with short prompts runs EAGLE with gamma = 4. After traffic doubled, the mean acceptance length is unchanged but the ITL gain from speculation disappeared. What is the most likely cause?
options: The draft head drifted and now proposes worse tokens
Larger batches pushed B x (gamma + 1) token rows past the ridge, so each verify pass now costs several plain steps
The KV cache of rejected tokens is no longer freed
Acceptance length always falls when traffic rises, so the metric must be broken
explain: Acceptance length measures the draft, and it did not change. What changed is the cost of a verify pass: with short contexts the step becomes compute bound once B(gamma + 1) approaches about 153 rows on an A100. Lowering gamma under load (dynamic speculation) or disabling it at high concurrency recovers the loss.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
question: In Whisper-Streaming you raise MinChunkSize, the minimum new audio processed per update. What happens?
options: Latency rises, but each update sees more audio, so quality tends to improve
Latency drops, because fewer updates are needed
Nothing, because LocalAgreement only depends on text
WER rises, because the 30 s window overflows
explain: The paper describes MinChunkSize as the parameter that controls latency and quality. Bigger chunks mean waiting longer before each update, but each transcription has more context. The paper also found the computationally unaware latency (ignoring compute time) to be about twice the chunk size, since two consecutive updates must agree. Buffers are trimmed at sentence ends to stay near 30 s, so overflow is not the issue.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
question: A program maps 1 GiB of memory and touches all of it with 4 KiB pages. Roughly how much memory do the last-level page tables alone take?
options: 4 KiB
64 KiB
2 MiB
1 GiB
explain: 1 GiB / 4 KiB = 262,144 page-table entries at 8 bytes each = 2 MiB, which is 512 PTE tables of 4 KiB. With 2 MiB pages the same gigabyte needs just 512 PMD entries, one 4 KiB table.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream
question: Why can a vector added only at layer l change the model's next-token prediction?
options: Because the model recomputes all earlier layers after the addition
Because the residual stream is a running sum: later layers read the shifted stream and the unembedding reads its final value
Because the vector is also added to the weights of every later layer
It cannot; the vector must be added at the last layer to matter
explain: Each block adds its output to the stream it reads, so a vector added at layer l stays in the sum. Later attention and MLP layers read it and react to it, and the final stream is what the unembedding decodes. No weights change and earlier layers are not rerun.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
question: Your refusal-steered model keeps its MMLU score, yet users report rambling, repetitive answers. Which check would have caught this?
options: Raising the coefficient
Measuring loss or KL on ordinary prompts and reading open-ended generations, not just multiple-choice accuracy
Running MMLU with more subjects
Using a single contrast pair instead of many
explain: MMLU in the A/B format reads one token's probability, which can survive while generation quality collapses. CAA saw exactly this: multiple-choice capability held while larger multipliers degraded open-ended text. Loss on ordinary text, KL on unrelated prompts and reading samples catch it.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
question: A gateway loses its uplink for 30 s and then forwards all buffered readings at once. You compute per-10 s averages by processing time. What happens to the 30 s of readings?
options: They are averaged into the windows in which they were measured, just later
They all land in the single window in which they arrived, and the three earlier windows show missing data
Kafka reorders them by event time before the processor sees them
MQTT QoS 1 guarantees they are delivered in event-time order
explain: Processing-time windows bucket by arrival. The burst lands in one window (inflating its count) and the earlier windows look empty. Kafka keeps the order in which records were written to a partition; it does not sort by event time.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
question: Which design gives the most useful long-term history for detecting rare overheating at the lowest storage cost?
options: Keep raw readings forever
Keep raw data for days and 1-minute rollups with count, mean, min and max for years
Keep only 1-hour means for years
Keep only the latest reading per sensor
explain: Short raw retention covers debugging, and long-lived rollups with min and max keep the extremes that a mean hides, at a fraction of the rows. Hourly means alone would average away a 30 second overheat.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Multi-head attention by hand: two heads, two patterns
question: In "the cat sat because it was tired", the query row for "it" puts 0.85 on "because" in head 1, and 0.70 on "cat" in head 2. Which head helps the model work out what "it" refers to?
options: Head 2, because it links the pronoun to the noun it stands for
Head 1, because its weight is higher, so it is more confident
Neither, because attention weights cannot carry meaning between words
Both equally, because the head outputs are concatenated
explain: Resolving "it" means finding its noun, and head 2 sends most of the weight there. Head 1 is a previous-token pattern: useful for local structure, not for reference. A higher weight only says the head is confident, not that it is doing this job. Concatenation keeps the heads' outputs separate; it does not make them equal.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: One layer end to end, in numbers and in code, and how it decodes
question: An encoder-decoder translates a 12-token sentence into 15 tokens with greedy decoding (plus one end token). How many times does the encoder stack run?
options: 16 times, once per decoder step
Once; every decoder step cross-attends to the same stored encoder output
12 times, once per source token
28 times, once per source and per target token
explain: The source does not change while decoding, so the encoder runs once and its output z is reused by cross-attention at every step. The decoder runs once per generated token (16 here).

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
question: Under b = 0.75, avgdl = 20, k1 = 1.2, what is K = k1 x B for a 40-token document?
options: 1.2, the same as k1
2.4, because the document is twice the average
0.6, because long documents saturate sooner
explain: B = 0.25 + 0.75 x (40/20) = 1.75, so K = 1.2 x 1.75 = 2.1. It is not 2.4 because only the b share of B scales with length; the (1 - b) share stays fixed. A larger K means the long document needs more occurrences to reach the same factor, not fewer.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
question: For GPT-2 small, roughly what share of all parameters sits in the MLPs?
options: About 10%
About 23%
About 45%
About 31%
explain: The MLPs have 8C^2 + 5C per block, twice attention's 4C^2 + 4C, totalling 56.67M of 124.44M, which is 45.5%. 23% is attention and 31% is the token embedding table.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Making it fast: TF32, bfloat16, torch.compile, fused attention and DDP
question: Which of these changes alters the numbers the model computes, not just how fast it computes them?
options: Switching from manual attention to scaled_dot_product_attention
Moving matmuls from float32 to TF32 or bfloat16
Wrapping the model in DDP with gradients averaged across 8 GPUs
Fusing AdamW into one kernel
explain: Lower-precision formats round the matmul inputs, so results differ slightly from float32; that is the accuracy traded for speed. Fused attention computes the same function (we saw agreement to 7e-7), DDP's averaged gradient equals one big batch's, and a fused optimizer does the same update.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
question: What is the derivative of softplus $\ln(1 + e^z)$ at $z = 0$?
options: 0, because ReLU has slope 0 to the left of 0
1, because softplus is a version of ReLU
0.5, because the slope of softplus is the sigmoid and $\sigma(0) = 0.5$
About 0.693, the value of softplus at 0
explain: The chain rule gives $\zeta'(z) = e^z/(1 + e^z) = \sigma(z)$, and $\sigma(0) = 1/2$. 0.693 is $\ln 2$, the height of softplus at 0, not its slope. Unlike ReLU, softplus has no corner, so its slope at 0 is well defined.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Second derivatives, the Hessian and the shape of a minimum
question: At a critical point the Hessian has eigenvalues 4 and -1. What kind of point is it?
options: A saddle point: the function curves up along one eigenvector and down along the other
A local minimum, because the larger eigenvalue is positive
A local maximum, because one eigenvalue is negative
Cannot tell without the gradient
explain: Mixed signs mean the point is a minimum along one direction and a maximum along another: a saddle. A minimum needs every eigenvalue positive. The gradient is already known to be zero at a critical point, so it adds nothing.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait
question: You type `deploy` and get `command not found` with status 127, yet `ls -l ~/bin/deploy` shows the file exists with mode `-rwxr-xr-x`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The file needs a .sh extension
Exit status 127 means the program crashed while starting
`~/bin` is not one of the directories in PATH
Bash only searches PATH for builtins
explain: Names without a slash are only looked up in the PATH directories. Add the directory to PATH or call it by path, `~/bin/deploy`. Extensions mean nothing to the kernel, and a crash would give a different status.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Pipes: concurrent processes, sort | uniq -c, and SIGPIPE
question: Which pipeline lists the 3 most common words in words.txt (one word per line)?
options: `uniq -c words.txt | sort -rn | head -n 3`
`sort words.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3`
`sort -rn words.txt | uniq -c | head -n 3`
`sort words.txt | head -n 3 | uniq -c`
explain: Sort first so equal words are adjacent, count with uniq -c, then sort the counts numerically in reverse and take 3. The third option sorts the words themselves, not counts, and the last one cuts the data before counting.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: From one-hot IDs to a trainable embedding table
question: A batch contains the token IDs [2, 2, 4] and the model uses an embedding table with 5 rows. After one backward pass, which rows of the table have a nonzero gradient?
options: All 5 rows, because the whole matrix is a parameter
Rows 2 and 4, with row 2's gradient being the sum of two contributions
Rows 2 and 4, with row 2's gradient counted once because duplicates are removed
Only row 4, because repeated tokens cancel out
explain: Only looked-up rows get gradient, and a row looked up twice accumulates both contributions (the lookup's backward pass is a scatter-add: each position's gradient is added into the row its ID points to, so repeats sum). Rows 0, 1 and 3 get exactly zero, which is what makes sparse updates possible.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Train word2vec yourself: SGNS in PyTorch, then gensim
question: You reproduce a skip-gram result with gensim's `Word2Vec`, passing `vector_size=100`, `negative=5` and `ns_exponent=0.75` and leaving every other argument at its default. Your scores do not match the reference. Which setting is most likely wrong?
options: `ns_exponent=0.75`
`negative=5`
`vector_size=100`
`sg` was left at its default 0, so it trained CBOW
explain: With `sg` left at its default 0, gensim trains CBOW, which predicts the center from averaged context vectors. The three settings you passed are valid skip-gram values (5 negatives and the 3/4 exponent are the paper's choices). CBOW is a fine model, but it is a different one, so results will not match a skip-gram reference.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Where word vectors fail: unseen words, many senses and bias
question: A support chatbot built on static word vectors treats *Apple* the fruit and *Apple* the company identically. What does this lesson suggest?
options: Increase the vector dimension so both senses fit
Use contextual embeddings, which compute a separate vector per occurrence
Train with more negative samples
Use hierarchical softmax instead of negative sampling
explain: A static table has one row per word, so every sense shares it whatever the dimension or training objective. Contextual models compute a vector from each sentence, so the two uses differ.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Math-bound or memory-bound: arithmetic intensity and the roofline
question: Elementwise operations (add, ReLU, LayerNorm) are at most a few FLOP/B. What is the standard way to make them cheaper on a GPU?
options: Use more Tensor Cores
Fuse them into the neighbouring kernel so the data is not written to and re-read from HBM
Increase the clock speed
Split them across more thread blocks
explain: They are memory-bound, so the only lever is fewer bytes moved. Fusing several elementwise steps into one kernel keeps the intermediate values on chip. More math units do not help a memory-bound operation.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Batching: sharing each weight read across many users
question: Why does continuous batching improve throughput over static batching?
options: Finished requests free their slot right away and waiting requests join at the next step, so fewer slots sit idle
It makes each decode step faster
It removes the need for a KV cache
It runs prefill and decode on different GPUs
explain: The step time is unchanged; what changes is how full the batch is. Iteration-level scheduling refills slots every iteration instead of waiting for the longest request.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Bits, bytes and hex: how numbers are stored
question: An `int` holding `0x12345678` is stored at address 0x100 on x86-64. Which byte is at address 0x100?
explain: x86-64 is little-endian: the least significant byte, 0x78, goes at the lowest address, followed by 0x56, 0x34 and 0x12 at 0x101 to 0x103. A big-endian machine would put 0x12 first.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why real CPUs beat the simple loop: pipelines and prediction
question: A profile shows a hot loop whose `if` on input data is mispredicted about half the time. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Add a few more instructions before the if so the CPU has time to think
Make the outcome predictable or branch-free, for example sort or group the data, or let the compiler use a conditional move
Split the loop across two functions
Turn off out-of-order execution
explain: The cost comes from flushing the pipeline on each wrong guess. Removing the guess (a conditional move) or making it right almost every time (sorted or grouped data) removes the penalty. Extra instructions or function boundaries do not make the direction any easier to predict.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
question: Using C of about 6ND, a 7B-parameter model trained on 2 trillion tokens needs roughly how many FLOPs?
explain: 6 x 7e9 x 2e12 = 8.4e22. The rule ignores attention's context-length term, which Kaplan et al. note is small when the model width is large relative to the context.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Policy gradients: how a score becomes a gradient
question: A policy samples response C, which has reward -1, with probabilities p = (0.426, 0.258, 0.316) over A, B, C. Without a baseline, how does this one sample move the three logits under gradient ascent?
options: It raises all three logits, because the gradient of a probability is always positive
It lowers C's logit and raises A's and B's, since r times (onehot(C) - p) = (0.426, 0.258, -0.684)
It raises C's logit, because C was the response sampled
It leaves the logits unchanged, because negative rewards give no gradient
explain: The sample's contribution is r(C) times (onehot(C) - p) = -1 times (-0.426, -0.258, 0.684). Ascent lowers C's logit by the largest amount and lifts the others. A negative reward acts like a push away from what was sampled.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
question: Why does an inverted index keep each postings list sorted by docID?
options: So that the most relevant documents come first
So two lists can be intersected by walking them once, side by side
Because docIDs must be unique
So the dictionary can be binary searched
explain: A single global sort order lets the query engine merge two lists in one linear pass (lesson 3). Sorting by docID says nothing about relevance; ranking is a separate step. Binary search over the dictionary concerns terms, not postings.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Ranking with vectors and cosine similarity
question: Why do engines store the integer tf in each posting instead of the final tf-idf weight?
options: Because idf depends on df and N, which change as documents are added, and an integer is cheaper to store than a float
Because floats cannot be sorted
Because tf-idf weights are always integers anyway
Because cosine similarity ignores idf
explain: idf is a collection-wide statistic, so a stored tf-idf float would go stale every time the collection changes. A small integer tf also compresses far better than a float. The engine combines tf with the current idf at query time.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores
question: Given `int x = 5; int *p = &x; int **pp = &p; **pp = 9;`, what is the value of x?
options: 5, because only pp was assigned
It is undefined behavior
The address of p
explain: *pp is the object pp points to, which is p. **pp follows p one more step, reaching x. Assigning 9 through it writes into x. All of this is well defined because every pointer points to a live object of the right type.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
question: After `free(p);` the program later runs `free(p);` again. What does the C standard say happens?
options: The second call does nothing, like free(NULL)
The behavior is undefined
free returns an error code
The memory is freed twice, which is harmless
explain: free on a block that has already been deallocated is explicitly undefined behavior. Only a null pointer is a guaranteed no-op, which is why some code writes `free(p); p = NULL;`.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
question: An ASan report says `heap-use-after-free ... READ of size 4 ... in main uaf.c:7` and `freed by thread T0 here: ... in main uaf.c:6`. What is the bug?
options: Line 7 reads through a pointer whose block was freed on line 6
Line 6 frees a pointer that malloc never returned
Line 7 reads an uninitialized local variable on the stack
The program ran out of heap memory
explain: ASan reports the bad access (line 7), plus where the block was freed (line 6) and allocated. Reading 4 bytes after free is a use after free. The fix is to finish using the data before freeing it, or not to free it yet.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1
options: None; `drop` is special and can be called twice
`drop(s)`, because the first iteration moves `s` into `drop` and the second iteration uses a moved value
`for _ in 0..2`, because loops cannot capture Strings
explain: `drop` is an ordinary function taking its argument by value, so the first call moves `s`. The compiler sees the loop can run again and reports E0382 (use of moved value). This is a double free the compiler caught.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Lifetimes: tying a returned reference to its inputs
question: Which signature compiles **without** explicit lifetime annotations?
options: `fn pick(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str`
`fn make() -> &str`
`fn get(&self, key: &str) -> &str` (a method)
explain: Rule 3: the output takes the lifetime of `&self`. Options 1 and 4 have two input lifetimes and no receiver, and option 2 has no input lifetime at all, so elision cannot fill in the output in any of them (E0106).

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
question: You store 1,000 user profiles, each with 32 numeric features, as vectors. Which statement is right?
options: Each profile is a vector in R^1000
You cannot add two profiles because their features have different meanings
Each profile is a vector in R^32, and you can add two profiles component by component
Each feature is a vector in R^32
explain: Each profile has 32 components, so it lives in $\mathbb{R}^{32}$. The math allows adding any two vectors of the same dimension; whether the sum is *meaningful* depends on the features, but averaging profiles (add, then scale by 1/2) is a common and legal operation.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Span, independence and rank: what a matrix can reach
question: Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$: $[1,0]$, $[0,1]$ and $[1,1]$. Which statement is right?
options: They are linearly independent, because no two of them are parallel
Their span is 3-dimensional, one dimension per vector
They are linearly dependent, and their span is the whole plane
They are dependent, so their span is only a line
explain: $[1,1] = [1,0] + [0,1]$, so the set is dependent, but the first two already reach every point of the plane. No two being parallel is not enough for independence. The plane has dimension 2, so no set of 3 vectors in it can be independent, and no span inside it can be 3-dimensional.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Tensors, batches and broadcasting: shapes in real code
question: Arrays of shape (8, 1, 6) and (7, 6) are added. What is the result's shape?
options: An error, because they have different numbers of axes
explain: Pad the shorter shape on the left: (1, 7, 6). Compare from the right: 6 and 6 match, 1 and 7 give 7, 8 and 1 give 8. Result (8, 7, 6). Different numbers of axes are fine; missing axes count as size 1.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Many features: linear regression in matrix form and feature scaling
question: A model uses income in USD (values around 50,000) and age in years (around 40). Gradient descent needs a tiny learning rate and the age weight barely moves. What is the best first fix?
options: Use a much larger learning rate
Drop the age feature
Train for more epochs
Standardize both features using training-set means and standard deviations
explain: Income's huge scale makes its curvature, and so the largest Hessian eigenvalue, enormous, which caps the safe learning rate; age then crawls. Standardizing equalizes the scales. A larger rate would diverge along the income direction, and more epochs only wait out the crawl.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Validation and penalties: choosing lambda, L2 and L1
question: With SGD and learning rate 0.1, an L2 term $\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2$ with $\lambda = 0.0005$ shrinks each weight by what factor before the gradient step?
explain: The step is $w \leftarrow (1 - 2\eta\lambda)w - \eta\nabla L$, and $2 \times 0.1 \times 0.0005 = 0.0001$, so the factor is $0.9999$. Note the factor 2 from differentiating $\lambda w^2$; many libraries define the penalty with a $\tfrac{1}{2}$ to cancel it.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Build it: a complete training loop in NumPy
question: Someone runs this code with lam = 1.0 instead of 0.001. Validation loss stalls at about 0.63 and the weights end near (0.13, 0.13). What happened?
options: The penalty dominates the loss, shrinking the weights so much that predictions stay near 0.5: underfitting
The model overfits because lambda is large
Early stopping fired too late
The data were not shuffled
explain: With $\lambda = 1$ the term $\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2$ outweighs the gain from fitting, so the weights stay tiny, every $p$ stays near 0.5, and the loss stays close to $\ln 2 = 0.693$. Strong regularization trades variance for bias, and here bias wins. Choose $\lambda$ on validation data.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The chain rule on a computational graph
question: In the forward pass $m = \max(a, b)$ with $a = 4$ and $b = 1$. The upstream gradient is $\partial L/\partial m = 2$. What are $\partial L/\partial a$ and $\partial L/\partial b$?
options: 1 and 1
2 and 2
2 and 0
1.6 and 0.4, split by size
explain: Max routes the gradient: only the input that won (a = 4) affects m, so it gets the full upstream gradient 2. Nudging b slightly does not change m at all, so its gradient is 0.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradients through depth: vanishing, exploding and unlucky seeds
question: A layer has 256 inputs and 64 outputs. Which weight variance does Glorot initialisation use, and which condition does each width come from?
options: $1/256$: only the forward pass matters
$2/320 = 1/160$: 256 from keeping activations steady going forward, 64 from keeping errors steady going backward
$2/64$: He initialisation for the output width
$1/64$: only the backward pass matters
explain: Forward, a unit sums 256 inputs, so steady activations need $256\,v = 1$. Backward, BP2 sums over the 64 units each input feeds, so steady errors need $64\,v = 1$. Glorot averages the widths: $v = 2/(256 + 64) = 1/160$.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: CPU scheduling: turnaround time versus response time
question: Three 5-second jobs arrive together. You switch from SJF to round robin with a 1 s slice. What happens to average turnaround and average response time?
options: Both improve
Turnaround gets worse (10 s to 14 s) and response gets better (5 s to 1 s)
Turnaround improves and response gets worse
Both stay the same because the total work is unchanged
explain: RR starts every job almost immediately, so average response drops from 5 s to 1 s. But it interleaves the jobs, so all of them finish near the end: 13, 14 and 15 s, averaging 14 s versus SJF's 10 s. Fairness over short time scales costs turnaround.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Waiting for something: condition variables and semaphores
question: A bounded buffer has one producer and two consumers, one condition variable, and consumers that check `if (count == 0)` before waiting. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: with a lock held, if and while behave the same
A woken consumer can find the buffer already emptied by the other consumer and call get() on an empty buffer
The producer can overwrite a full buffer even with one consumer
The program deadlocks because wait() keeps the mutex
explain: Under Mesa semantics a wakeup is only a hint. Between the producer's signal and Tc1 running, Tc2 can take the item. With if, Tc1 does not re-check and calls get() on an empty buffer. wait() releases the mutex while sleeping, so the last option is wrong.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Files and directories: the API and how vsfs finds your data
question: With nothing cached, each directory fitting in one block, and the superblock in memory, how many disk reads does `open("/a/b/c")` cost?
explain: Root inode, root data, a's inode, a's data, b's inode, b's data, and finally c's inode: 7 reads. open() reads the target's inode but not its data; the data is read by later read() calls.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
question: You flip a fair coin twice. Let A = "first flip is heads" and B = "the two flips match". Are A and B independent?
options: No, because B depends on the first flip
Yes: P(A and B) = 1/4 = P(A) P(B)
No, because A and B can both happen
It cannot be determined without more data
explain: P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 2/4 = 1/2 (HH or TT), and P(A and B) = P(HH) = 1/4 = P(A)P(B). Even though B is defined using the first flip, it is independent of A. Independence is checked with numbers, not by whether one event is mentioned in the other's definition.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Why averages are stable: the law of large numbers and the CLT
question: Batch size 64 gives a gradient-estimate standard deviation of s (per coordinate, i.i.d. examples). Approximately what does batch size 256 give?
options: s, since batch size does not affect noise
explain: The mini-batch gradient is an average of per-example gradients, so its standard deviation scales as 1/sqrt(batch). Four times the batch gives sqrt(4) = 2 times less noise, so s/2. The variance falls by 4.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayesian estimation: priors, posteriors and MAP
question: Prior Beta(3, 3). You observe 2 heads and 6 tails. What are the posterior and its MAP estimate?
options: Beta(5, 9), MAP 1/3
Beta(2, 6), MAP 0.25
Beta(5, 9), MAP 0.25, the same as the MLE
Beta(3, 3), since one small sample does not change the prior
explain: Add heads to a and tails to b: Beta(3 + 2, 3 + 6) = Beta(5, 9). MAP = (5 - 1) / (5 + 9 - 2) = 4/12 = 1/3, pulled from the MLE of 0.25 toward the prior's 0.5.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
question: Your budget is fixed. You decide to make the model 3 times larger than planned. What must happen to the number of training tokens?
options: It stays the same, compute depends only on N
It must triple
It must drop to one third
It must drop to one ninth
explain: With $C \approx 6ND$ fixed, $D = C/(6N)$, so tripling N cuts D to one third. Compute depends on both knobs; nothing about the product is squared.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Kaplan vs Chinchilla: why 2020-era models were undertrained
question: Which is the best summary of the Kaplan vs Chinchilla disagreement?
options: Chinchilla showed loss does not follow power laws
They agree that loss is a power law, but differ on how to split compute; replications trace Kaplan's split to experimental setup
Kaplan used more compute so its result is more reliable
The difference is only because they used different tokenizers
explain: Both papers find smooth power-law trends. The disagreement is the compute-optimal exponent (0.73 vs about 0.5), and later work explains it by schedule, parameter counting, small scale and optimizer details. Kaplan actually used smaller models than Chinchilla.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
question: A query has exactly 3 relevant documents in the qrels. A perfect system ranks all 3 first. What are its P@10 and R@10?
explain: Recall is 3/3 = 1.0 because every relevant document is retrieved. Precision at 10 counts all 10 slots, and only 3 can ever be relevant, so it is 0.3 even for a perfect ranking. This is why P@k is hard to average across queries with different numbers of relevant documents.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine
question: Your vectors are L2-normalized at indexing time and queries are normalized too. A teammate switches the scoring function from cosine to dot product to save time. What happens to the ranking?
options: It is identical, because for unit vectors the dot product equals the cosine
It changes, because dot product favors longer documents
It reverses
It becomes random
explain: Cosine divides the dot product by the two lengths. When both lengths are 1, that division does nothing, so the scores and the ranking are identical. This is exactly why normalizing once is standard practice.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
question: Starting from the initial corpus, suppose newest appeared 9 times instead of 6 (everything else unchanged). Which pair would be merged first?
options: (e, s), still tied with (s, t) and (t, _) at 12
(l, o), because low is the most frequent word
(w, e), which rises to 11
(n, e), because newest is now the most frequent word
explain: Each of (e, s), (s, t), (t, _) becomes $9 + 3 = 12$, and (w, e) becomes $9 + 2 = 11$. The top count is a three-way tie at 12, and the first-seen rule picks (e, s). Word frequency alone does not decide: (l, o) gets 7 and (n, e) gets 9.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Special tokens, chat templates and prompt boundaries
question: A service builds each prompt as system_text + user_text and encodes it with `enc.encode(prompt, allowed_special="all")`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; allowed_special only changes how decoding works
It is slower, but the ids are identical either way
It raises ValueError on every prompt
A user who types a special string such as <|endoftext|> gets the real control token, so their text can end the document or fake structure the model trusts
explain: allowed_special="all" turns every special string in the text into its control id, including strings typed by users. Allow special tokens only in text you wrote, and encode user text with the defaults (which raise) or with disallowed_special=() so it stays plain text.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
question: Why does He initialization use 2 / fan-in rather than Xavier's 1 / fan-in (equal fans) for ReLU layers?
options: ReLU doubles the gradient on the positive side
The factor 2 accounts for the bias term
ReLU zeroes about half of a symmetric pre-activation, halving the mean square, and the factor 2 cancels that
Larger weights train faster, so 2 is a safe speed-up
explain: With zero-mean symmetric pre-activations, ReLU keeps only the positive half, so the average of $\mathrm{relu}(z)^2$ is $\mathrm{Var}(z)/2$. Multiplying Var(w) by 2 restores a per-layer factor of exactly 1.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Mixed precision: fp16, bf16 and loss scaling
question: Your gradients include many values around 1e-9 and you want to avoid a loss scaler. Which format works, and what does it give up?
options: fp16, because subnormals reach down past 1e-9
bf16: fp32's exponent range keeps 1e-9 representable, at the cost of only 7 mantissa bits (spacing 0.0078 near 1)
fp16, because it has more mantissa bits than bf16
Either one: both have 8 exponent bits
explain: fp16's smallest positive number is 2^-24, about 6e-8, so 1e-9 rounds to 0 unless the loss is scaled. bf16 keeps fp32's 8 exponent bits, so range is not the problem; precision is, which is why the weights stay in fp32.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Instrumenting a run: gradient norms, update ratios, activation stats
question: A run's loss sits at 2.30 (10 classes) for 300 steps. Every layer's update-to-weight ratio is about 1e-8, and the activation std drops about 8x per layer. Most likely cause?
options: Weights initialized far too small, so the signal and gradients vanish
A learning rate 30x too high
model.eval() was never called
Dropout is too strong
explain: A constant ln 10 loss means the network predicts uniformly. The per-layer scale collapse matches lesson 1's analysis of a too-small init, and ratios of 1e-8 mean the weights are effectively frozen. A too-high rate gives large ratios and climbing gradient norms instead.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Building the graph: insertion and the neighbor heuristic
question: Which change increases index build time but leaves query-time cost per ef roughly the same?
options: Raising ef at query time
Raising ef_construction
Raising M
Raising the dimension d
explain: ef_construction only controls the beam width during inserts. M also raises query cost because every expanded node has more neighbors to score; d makes every distance more expensive; ef is the query knob itself.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Install scripts: why installing a package runs its code
question: Which of these runs a third-party package's own code on your machine before your application ever imports it?
options: Installing an npm package that has a postinstall script, with scripts enabled
Reading the package's README on the registry website
Running npm ls
Installing a pure-Python wheel with pip
explain: Lifecycle scripts run during install. A wheel is unpacked without running package code (though a .pth file it installs runs at the next Python start).

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Build system compromise: SolarWinds, CCleaner and 3CX
question: SUNSPOT replaced a source file only while MsBuild was running and restored it afterwards. Which check would most likely have exposed it?
options: Verifying the code-signing signature on the shipped DLL (dynamic-link library, a Windows code file)
Code review of the git repository
Running unit tests
Rebuilding the same commit on an independent builder and comparing hashes
explain: The repository was clean and the signature was genuine. Only something that compares the build output against an independent build of the same source sees the difference.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Signing artifacts: from long-lived keys to Sigstore
question: Why does keyless signing reduce the damage of a CI compromise compared with a GPG key stored as a CI secret?
options: Fulcio scans artifacts for malware before signing
There is no long-lived private key to steal; each key lives for one signature, and every signing event is publicly logged
Keyless signatures do not need verification
Sigstore signatures cannot be forged even by the signer
explain: An attacker inside the job could still sign during that run, but they cannot walk away with a key that works for months, and their signing is visible in Rekor. Compare HashiCorp's forced key rotation after Codecov.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils I: two years of patient social engineering
question: Which control would most directly have stopped Jia Tan from shipping 5.6.0 alone?
options: Running unit tests in CI
Signing release tarballs
Requiring a second maintainer to review and approve every release and the release archive contents
Using SHA-256 instead of CRC in xz
explain: The releases were signed and tests passed. A second, independent person checking that the release archive matched the reviewed git tree is the control aimed at a single trusted insider, which SLSA's Source track formalises as required review.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Language models: decoding cuts the tail, scaling stalls
question: You generate 10x more synthetic training text from the same teacher with top-p 0.9. Under the tail-cutting model, when does this stop improving the student?
options: Never: error keeps falling as a power law in T
Once T exceeds roughly k to the power beta, where k is the effective tail cut; after that error plateaus at the missing tail mass
Immediately: synthetic data never helps
Only when the teacher's perplexity exceeds the student's
explain: Data from a tail-cut generator only teaches the head of the distribution. Once the student has learned the head, the remaining error is the mass of the items it never sees, and more samples from the same generator cannot reveal them.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
question: A lab wants its 2027 pretraining mix to stay anchored to human text. Which plan does this lesson support best?
options: Keep pre-LLM snapshots and other known-human sources permanently in the mix, and treat classifier or watermark filtering of new crawls as an extra layer
Rely on an AI-text classifier to remove all model-written pages from new crawls, then drop the old snapshots to save space
Rely on watermarks, since every model that writes web text embeds one
Ignore provenance, since accumulating any data at all prevents every form of collapse
explain: Detectors can be evaded by paraphrasing and are bounded by how close AI text is to human text, and watermarks cover only cooperating generators. Known-human data kept permanently is the anchor that does not depend on detection. Accumulation bounds error but does not by itself protect the tails.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: mmap: putting a file into your address space
question: The 10,000-byte file is mapped writable with MAP_SHARED and length 12,288. You write p[10500] = 'x'. What happens?
options: SIGBUS, because byte 10,500 is past end of file
The file grows to 10,501 bytes
The write succeeds in memory but is never written to the file
SIGSEGV, because shared mappings cannot be written past EOF
explain: Byte 10,500 is in page 2, the last partial page, so it is mapped and zero-filled. mmap(2) says modifications to that tail region are not written out to the file. mmap never changes a file's size; use ftruncate first if you need the file to grow. SIGBUS would only come from touching page 3, which is wholly beyond EOF.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Watching and restricting system calls: strace, faults and seccomp
question: strace -c on a busy program shows 2 million read calls taking 4 s of system time. Without strace, the program's total run time is 1.5 s. What is the best reading?
options: The program spends 4 s in read; strace measures it exactly
strace double-counts calls made by threads
read must be served by the vDSO in the untraced run
The call count is trustworthy, but strace's own overhead inflates the times, so measure time without it
explain: Tracing stops the program around every call, so times under strace are inflated; strace(1) warns that a traced process runs more slowly. The count of 2 million is what the program really does, and it suggests a bigger buffer. read has no vDSO version.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Taming the tail: hedged requests and honest reporting
question: Your team wants a fleet-wide p99 dashboard. Each of 40 hosts exports its own p99 every minute. What should you do?
options: Average the 40 p99 values, weighting by request count
Take the maximum of the 40 p99 values, which is exactly the fleet p99
Export histogram bucket counts from each host, sum them, and compute p99 from the merged histogram
Take the median of the 40 p99 values to ignore outlier hosts
explain: Percentiles are not additive; neither the weighted mean nor the max of per-host p99s equals the fleet p99 in general. Summed histogram counts describe the combined distribution, so the percentile computed from them is right up to bucket resolution.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Allen relations, current roles and time-scoped queries
question: At month granularity with half-open intervals, role X is Jan 2020 to Jun 2020 and role Y is Jul 2020 to Dec 2020 (both as written, inclusive). Which Allen relation holds for X relative to Y?
options: before, because June is before July
overlaps, because they share the month boundary
during
meets
explain: As half-open intervals X is [2020-01, 2020-07) and Y is [2020-07, 2021-01). X's exclusive end equals Y's start, which is the definition of meets: back-to-back, no gap and no overlap.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Precision: majority vote, best-of-N and when they plateau
question: Your majority-vote accuracy on a math benchmark stops improving between N = 64 and N = 512, but pass@512 (checked against the answer key) keeps rising. What is the most likely reason?
options: Samples become correlated at large N
On the unsolved problems the correct answer is a minority answer, so adding votes reinforces the wrong mode
The model runs out of context window
pass@k is computed incorrectly at large N
explain: Majority vote converges to the mode of the answer distribution. For problems where a wrong answer is the mode, more samples raise coverage but not voting accuracy. That is the plateau Brown et al. report.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
question: DeepSeek-R1-Zero's responses became much longer during RL even though no reward term asked for length. Why is that evidence for test-time scaling?
options: Longer outputs are always rewarded by GRPO
Length was capped at 1,000 tokens
The model copied long human traces
The reward was only for correctness and format, so the model discovered that spending more tokens per problem raised its success rate
explain: R1-Zero's rewards were rule-based accuracy and format rewards. Growth in thinking length alongside accuracy shows the policy learned to buy correctness with test-time tokens.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
question: Which of these changes the trained weights of a network itself at inference, instead of a per-sequence state that starts fresh for every input?
options: A TTT-Linear layer reading a 10,000-token prompt
Linear attention accumulating v k-transpose over a document
LaCT updating its SwiGLU fast weights once per 2048-token chunk
Sun et al. (2019): one rotation-prediction gradient step on each test image before classifying it
explain: Sun et al. update the classifier's own shared parameters with a self-supervised loss on the test image. The other three are fast weights: a TTT layer's W, linear attention's state and LaCT's fast weights all start from a learned or zero initial value for each sequence and are thrown away afterwards, while the network's ordinary weights stay frozen.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans' three architectures, worked one segment at a time
question: In MAC, why does segment 3's attention not see the memory update made from segment 3's own tokens?
options: Because the memory is read before the segment is written: h comes from M_2, and the write that adds segment 3 happens after attention
Because MAC never writes segment tokens into the memory
Because persistent tokens block the memory during segment 3
Because the memory is only updated at the end of the sequence
explain: MAC's order is retrieve, attend, write, gate. Retrieval reads M_(t-1), from before the segment, so attention combines the compressed past with the exact current segment. Only the final gate reads the freshly written M_t.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: One lock, many cores: why a shared slab cache stops scaling
question: A service spends 50 ns per malloc inside a global allocator lock. Ignoring everything else, what is the most mallocs per second the whole machine can do through that lock?
options: 20 million per second, regardless of core count
20 million per second per core
It depends only on how fast each core runs application code
Unlimited, since a mutex costs nothing when uncontended
explain: One holder at a time, 50 ns each: $1/(50 \text{ ns}) = 2 \times 10^7$ per second for the whole machine. More cores add waiters, not throughput.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
question: An application runs 4,000 threads on a 32-CPU machine, most of them blocked most of the time. Which allocator front-end is the better fit for memory footprint, and why?
options: Per-thread caches, because blocked threads release their caches automatically
Per-CPU caches, because the number of caches is bounded by the 32 CPUs rather than the 4,000 threads
Neither: a global lock is best when threads are mostly blocked
Per-thread caches, because rseq does not work with more threads than CPUs
explain: Per-thread caches keep idle objects in every thread's cache, including the thousands of sleeping ones, or must shrink each cache until it is useless. Per-CPU caches exist only per logical CPU, so at most 32 hold memory, and the running threads share them.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Stacking: let the rare thing rise to the top
question: You stack 'process opened a handle to LSASS' across 3,000 machines. One backup agent made 50,000 such events, all on a single server, so sorted by count() it looks like the most common program. Which aggregation shows it is present on only one machine?
options: Sorting by time instead of by count
dcount(DeviceId) per process, the number of distinct devices
count() of events per process
sum of event sizes per process
explain: Counting distinct devices measures prevalence: a value seen on one device stays at 1 however many events that device produces, so the backup agent rises into the rare list next to the other one-machine programs, where a person can confirm it is the expected server. Counting raw events lets any chatty process look 'common' and sink out of a least-frequent list.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: An intelligence-driven hunt: living off the land and Volt Typhoon
question: A Volt Typhoon-style actor copied ntds.dit with ntdsutil and then deleted the copy. Which evidence from the hunt plan most likely still records where the copy was written?
options: Event 1102
ESENT events 216, 325, 326 and 327 in the Application log
The PortProxy registry key
The firewall log
explain: AA23-144A notes that the ESENT events' details should contain the file path where the copies were created, and that this 'can greatly aid in a hunt operation' because the files themselves can be deleted. Event 1102 would only show that a log was cleared, and the port proxy and firewall evidence concern a different behaviour.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Measuring a hunt programme, and where to practise
question: A hunt team spends a month hunting for encoded PowerShell, which already has a tested production rule that fires reliably. What does TaHiTI suggest they should have done first?
options: Checked the state of existing detections to avoid hunting for activity that traditional detection already covers
Hunted only for file hashes
Nothing; repeating hunts is always good
Bought a new EDR
explain: TaHiTI says continuous insight into the state of detection mechanisms is required 'to avoid hunting for malicious activity that is already covered'. Hunting time is scarce; spend it where the coverage map is empty or untested.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Collection: where intelligence comes from, and what it is worth
question: Your SOC confirmed 40 malicious domains last quarter. A paid feed of 2 million domains contained 12 of them, all also present in your free ISAC feed. What does this measurement show?
options: The paid feed is the most valuable because it is the largest
The paid feed added no unique detections against what you saw last quarter; check whether it serves another requirement before renewing
The ISAC feed must be wrong because it is smaller
Both feeds should be dropped because neither had all 40
explain: Unique contribution was zero against confirmed activity, so the feed's value, if any, lies elsewhere (another PIR, earlier delivery, or threats you have not yet seen). Size says nothing about relevance, and no feed will contain everything, so missing some confirmed domains is expected.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Kill chain and ATT&CK as analytic frames
question: A 2024 advisory tags log clearing as T1070.001. Your 2026 detection list (ATT&CK v20) has a rule tagged T1685.005. What is the right conclusion?
options: They are unrelated techniques
They describe the same behaviour under different ATT&CK versions; translate the ID before measuring coverage
The advisory is wrong
T1685.005 must be deprecated
explain: In ATT&CK v20, T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs redirects to T1685.005 under Disable or Modify Tools. Mappings are version-specific, so compare like with like.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Attribution: levels, evidence and its limits
question: In April 2021 the US named the SVR; in April 2022 Mandiant merged UNC2452 into APT29. Why might a vendor take a year longer than a government?
options: Vendors are not allowed to attribute
The vendor only reached the conclusion once its own firsthand evidence supported it, while the government could draw on intelligence sources a company does not have
The government statement was wrong
APT29 did not exist before 2022
explain: Mandiant said its merge was 'based on firsthand data gathered by Mandiant'. Governments can use signals and human intelligence that are not public, which supports the sponsor rung earlier but cannot be checked by outsiders.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Assets and adversaries: what is worth taking, and by whom
question: Your adversary list contains only 'anonymous internet attacker'. What does the model most likely miss?
options: Denial-of-service attacks
Attacks on the encryption of web traffic
Phishing emails
Misuse by people who already have legitimate access
explain: Insiders start inside the trust boundary with real credentials. Anonymous internet attackers can attempt denial of service, phishing and network attacks, so those are not the gap.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack trees: start from the attacker's goal
question: You can spend money on one defence. Which helps the root of an attack tree most?
options: Raising the cost of the branch that is currently cheapest
Raising the cost of the most expensive branch
Adding a new leaf to every branch
Whichever defence is cheapest to buy
explain: The root of an OR tree equals its cheapest branch. Raising any other branch leaves the root unchanged. Price matters, but only after you know which branch it changes.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
question: FireEye raised alerts on 30 November and 2 December, yet data kept leaving until mid-December. What does this teach about defence in depth?
options: A detection layer only counts if someone acts on it: detection without response is not a working layer
FireEye was the wrong product
Detection is useless against skilled attackers
Alerts should be turned off to reduce noise
explain: The signal was there. The response process failed. The next lesson shows why layers that share a failure, such as one ignored alert queue, add less protection than they appear to.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance
question: A CXL device is onlined through the dax kmem driver, but firmware provides no HMAT or CDAT performance data. Which tier does its node join?
options: memory_tier4, the same tier as DRAM, so it is never a demotion target
memory_tier22, from the kmem default adistance of 5 x 576 = 2880
The slowest possible tier, because it has no CPUs
None: the kernel refuses to online memory without performance data
explain: drivers/dax/kmem.c starts from MEMTIER_DEFAULT_DAX_ADISTANCE (5 x 576 = 2880) and only overrides it if a performance-based algorithm can compute one. 2880 / 128 = 22.5, so tier 22. Memory onlined as ordinary system RAM instead defaults to 576 and would share tier 4 with DRAM.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Naive, seasonal naive and simple exponential smoothing
question: On the test year, seasonal naive has MAE 24.25 and naive has MAE 37.92. What would most directly remove seasonal naive's remaining error on this series?
options: Use a smaller alpha
Switch from MAE to RMSE
Use only the last 12 months of training data
Add a trend term, since all its errors are positive by roughly one year of growth
explain: Every seasonal naive error is positive, between 19 and 30, close to 12 months x 2 per month = 24. That is a systematic bias from ignoring the trend. A method with both trend and season terms (Holt-Winters, next lesson) addresses it. Changing the metric changes the score, not the forecast.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: The TLS 1.3 handshake, message by message
question: Which handshake messages in TLS 1.3 can a passive observer read in plaintext?
options: ClientHello, ServerHello and Certificate
Only ClientHello and ServerHello
None; everything is encrypted from the first byte
All of them; only application data is encrypted
explain: RFC 9846 encrypts every handshake message after ServerHello. The two Hello messages must be in clear because the keys do not exist until both key shares have been exchanged.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Downgrade attacks: POODLE, BEAST, Logjam and the fixes
question: A server supports TLS 1.2 and SSL 3.0 and implements TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV. Interference on the path causes a browser to fall back and retry with SSL 3.0. What happens?
options: The server accepts SSL 3.0, because the client asked for it
The browser detects the attacker's TCP reset and alerts the user
The server silently upgrades the connection to TLS 1.2
The server sees the SCSV, knows it supports a higher version than offered, and aborts with inappropriate_fallback
explain: The SCSV tells the server "this is a fallback retry". If the server could have done better, a fallback means someone interfered, so it refuses.
